submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective, essentially context-free detector of a fixed English lexicon of describing and appearing: it fires on the naming/description verbs (called, named, dubbed, termed, described, defined, recognised/recognized, referred, branded, styled), the similarity words (like, such, resembles/resembled/resembling), the appearance words (face, faces, facial, voice, voices, look, looks, looked, expression, complexion, image, picture, shape, profile) and the mental-image verbs (imagined, envisioned, dreamed), more weakly on the quantifiers some, all, any, many and the large numerals million, thousand, hundred, billion, trillion, and on the continuation pieces 'itted', 'anned' and 'akes' (which is why a split 'knitted' or 'scanned' reaches the peak while the same word as a single token, e.g. 'fitted' or 'stakes', does not). It is silent on near-synonyms outside that list (similar, same, comparable, equivalent, appear, seem, form, appearance, figure, visage, label, titled, known, most, more, much, few, several, each, every), on gerund and plural forms (naming, styling, describing, images, pictures, hundreds, thousands, millions), and on concrete count nouns and proper names (cliff, lion, museum, cup, door, table, window, bread, milk, flower, paper, Paris, Japan, Germany), with the copula context ('was/is X') raising every member of the field roughly 0.5-1.0 above its neutral-sentence level.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The East Reservoir was built between 1871 and 1884 to supply the growing mill districts along the river. Its designers chose a gravity-fed layout, so that water enters at the northern weir and leaves through a chain of settling basins before reaching the pumping hall. The original brick vaults remain in place beneath the forecourt, and engineers inspecting them in 2009 found the mortar in good condition.

Maintenance follows a four-year cycle. In spring the inlet screens are lifted, cleaned by hand and returned to their channels. Sediment gathered in the first basin is dried on the adjoining beds, tested for heavy metals and then carried away by lorry. The second basin is drained only in dry summers, when demand from the town is low enough to allow a fortnight of work.

Staff write inspections into a bound ledger kept in the gatehouse. Entries record the date, the weather, the depth of silt and the condition of the valves. The ledger for 1962 notes that the eastern culvert was repaired after a winter flood, and that two of the outlet gates had begun to stick. A later hand added a note in pencil about a leak near the south pier, which was sealed the following June.

The pumping hall houses four beam engines, of which two remain in working order. Volunteers run them on open days, using steam raised in a small coal-fired boiler. The engines turn at twelve revolutions per minute and lift water into the upper cistern, from where it feeds the ornamental fountain in the park.

Heritage consultants surveyed the site in 1998 and recommended listing the engine house, the chimney and the boundary wall. The report described the engine house as the finest surviving example of its kind in the county, and urged that the timber roof be repaired before winter. Funding was approved three years later, and scaffolding stood over the nave for the better part of a decade.

The roof was rebuilt with oak from a managed wood in the next valley. The trusses were assembled on the ground, lifted by crane and pegged into position. Lead was rolled on site and dressed over the ridges by hand. Rainwater now runs into cast-iron hoppers and down pipes that carry it to the old cistern beneath the yard.

Wildlife surveys began in 2015. Bats roost in the roof void during summer, so work on the gutters is confined to the colder months. A colony of house martins nests under the eaves of the gatehouse, and the grass beside the top basin is left unmown until the chicks have flown. Volunteers monitor the site weekly and send records to the county recorder.

Visitors reach the reservoir by a footpath that follows the old railway line. The walk lasts about forty minutes from the village and passes a lime kiln, a quarry and a stand of beech trees. Guided tours run on the first Saturday of the month between April and October, and school groups are welcome by arrangement.

The trust that now cares for the site publishes a short guide annually. It explains the history of the works, the layout of the basins and the work of the volunteers. Copies are sold in the gatehouse, and the proceeds pay for tools, paint and the upkeep of the footpath.
